To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

commercially available culture media can be used to differentiate basal epithelial cells at the air-liquid interface, and that the differentiation media used was not the primary determinant of differentiation outcome.
the differentiation potential at the beginning of the culture is a more critical determinant of ciliation than the differentiation medium used.

basal cells from healthy donors, COPD patients, and PCD patients are able to differentiate into multiciliated and mucus-producing cells in an air-liquid interphase culture system using commercially available media.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of commercially available culture media in air-liquid interfaces for ciliated epithelial cell differentiation.
the development of an in vitro system to study the mechanisms underlying ciliated differentiation.
understanding the molecular basis of ciliated cell differentiation and the mechanisms of disease in the nasal epithelium, and we have developed a robust protocol to study these processes.

, while the differentiation medium is a key factor for ciliated differentiation, basal cell expansion in a basal medium containing Y-27632 is the most important factor in determining the outcome of ciliated differentiation.

The main takeaway from our work is that
basal cell expansion in 3T3 co-culture and differentiation in air-liquid culture are not dependent on specific commercially available media, but rather on the quality of the starting material.

basal cells can be differentiated at air-liquid interphase with a variety of commercially available culture media and that the differentiation protocol itself does not have major effects on the outcome.

the differentiation potential and basal cell expansion efficiency of the starting cultures are more critical factors in the success of the air-liquid interface cultures than the differentiation medium used.
